September 2011 # Debt doubts undermine confidence - Copper prices rose towards $9,900/t as August opened, only to drop precipitously due to investor panic over sovereign debt. The LME 3-month price fell to a low of $8,580/t but subsequently rebounded to over $9,250/t on 31st August. - The demand picture is clouded by it being too soon to be able to disentangle the seasonal slowdown this month from any effects of the financial and economic turmoil seen over the past month. However, spot premia are holding up well despite the increased uncertainty about the consumption outlook. - Supply growth has been modest this year, which will keep the market in deficit through Q3, as disruptions continue to plague miners. While Grasberg is now threatened by a strike following the resolution of the Escondida stoppage, lower ore grades are the main reason for underperformance so far. |The supply/deman

# Macro fears overshadow market fundamentals The economic and financial market turmoil unleashed Jul-Aug Low as % of Jul-Aug High 15% over the past month was preceded by a debt deal for Greece at the end of July. The relief at avoiding default, 10% aided by a weakening of the dollar ahead of the US Congress passing a debt limit extension, seems to have 5% increased risk appetite and helped fuel a rise in the LME 0% copper price to a 3½ month intra-day trading high of $9,860/t on 1st August. This rally turned out to be only a -5% prelude to a collapse. A week and a half selloff ensued, -10% driven by investor long liquidation triggered by panic in financial markets over sovereign debt. The rush to exit -15% from copper and other “risky” assets really gained -20% Al Cu Ni Pb Sn momentum after Standard & Poor’s downgraded the USA’s AAA debt rating by one notch on 5th August. The Data: CRU, LME downgrade came on the heels of revised GDP growth estimates that showed the US recession had been deeper and the recovery shallower than previously thought. The uncertainty over the demand outlook only increased in the wake of a weak ISM manufacturing survey, which raised fears that the US economy will could fall back into recession. The Greek bailout could not and will not solve the Eurozone’s problems but merely shifted the spotlight of the crisis onto other countries in the currency union. Italy and Spain were the next countries to appear on the bond market’s radar, with the bond yields on these nations’ government debt jumping relative to Germany. Both countries have much larger economies than Greece and would present a far greater bailout challenge. Although the European Central Bank stepped in to buy Italian and Spanish bonds, this failed to soothe investor nerves. The downgrade of the US also reverberated in Europe by raising the spectre of France’s debt rating being downgraded. The inability of the leaders of the Eurozone to grasp the nettle and solve the sovereign debt issues added to the uncertainty over the outlook for the global economy and therefore the demand for copper. In response to the drum beat of negative macroeconomic news, the 3-month copper price fell to an intra-day trading low on 10th August of $8,580/t, a 13% decline from the 1st August peak. However, compared to the other LME metals, copper saw the narrowest price range (11%) and had recovered almost 50% of the loss by the end of the month (using official 3-month prices as shown in the chart above). Tin fared the worst with prices down 20% and recovering only 20% of its loss by month end. Equities also saw a sharp downturn, with the S&P 500 falling to 17.6% below its July peak in August, versus the 13% peak-to-trough decline for copper.

The decline in copper prices was further exacerbated by a strengthening US dollar, which has averaged about 2% higher on a trade weighted basis in August compared to its low in late July. ## **SHFE price fell less than LME** Although SHFE prices followed LME prices down, they did not fall as far. SHFE 3-month prices held at just under $9,000/t (RMB66,000/t), while LME prices languished almost $100/t lower on average from 10th August to the 25th of the month. This period thus saw the widest and most sustained opening of the SHFE/LME arbitrage window since July last year. So far, though, there has been only a relatively modest increase in cancelled warrants in Asian LME warehouses, which we consider one of the best barometers for SHFE/LME arbitrage trade. Warrants totalling only 5,175t were cancelled through 31st August. Usually © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 16 September 2011 Copper Monitor www.crumonitor.com when the arbitrage window opens, the peak in the level of Asian LME cancelled warrants occurs about a month after the spread between SHFE and LME prices has hit its widest. So we expect to see more warrants cancelled over the next few weeks. We believe that Chinese imports will increase in the next few months as the “spare” cathode stocks built up in China earlier this year have largely been whittled down. According to our China office, stock levels at Shanghai bonded warehouse stocks have remained in a 300,000-350,000t range since June, down from the peak of about 570,000t in March. SHFE stocks have also fallen, to 102,258t by the end of August. arbitrage window open, given the significant decline in the LME price. The open arb was accompanied by a rise in the Chinese import premium to above $100/t, with traders particularly active in the market. Consumers appear to have refrained from buying much in the dip, principally because of the difficulties in obtaining financing according to CRU’s analysts in China. As the LME price has recovered, to a high of $9,275/t for 3-month on 31st August, it is likely that the arb will close due to a lag in the rise on SHFE. China is still structurally short of copper units, but scrap imports have been rising over the past few months as Chinese consumers and producers both seek to limit raw material costs. In addition, consumption has slowed seasonally from Q2 so the immediate need for refined meta

l is not huge. We do expect to see higher cathode imports over the next couple of months. However, we anticipate that any restocking in the country will be delayed to Q4 and into early 2012 ahead of increased demand in the New Year, with only modest buying on the dips in the interim. ## **Demand still outpacing supply** Global industrial production and copper consumption are both on course to decline seasonally in Q3 (see chart at right). While the real economy appears to be holding up at the moment, it is sentiment about the sustainability of world economic growth that has weighed heavily on copper prices. The latest Purchasing Managers Indices indicate stalling growth in all the major markets at a time when governments in industrialised countries are forcing themselves to cut spending to reduce budget deficits as consumers continue to deleverage. This combination of events is prompting businesses that survived the recession in Europe and the USA to hoard cash, as confidence that increased investment spending will pay off is conspicuous by its absence. However, the shortfall will accrue in China, where we expect imports to increase but only enough to narrow the country’s deficit towards 100,000t. The market in the rest of the world should be broadly in balance, as subdued production growth meets seasonally slower demand. ## **Little stock left to destock, as premia flatline in the USA and Europe** The spot markets in the USA and Europe have been well supplied with cathode over the past month, but not enough to pull down premia. Copper consumers in both regions destocked earlier this year. As the economic outlook deteriorates, consumers continue to put off rebuilding inventories. In addition to a lack of optimism, high financing costs deter consumers from carrying expensive copper on their books. Furthermore, the high levels of contract business consumers entered into for 2011 and relatively abundant scrap availability mean that some consumers continue to sell cathode back to the market. Consumers that have taken delivery of more cathode than current downstream production levels can absorb make up some of the sellers. The other

sellers are those consumers who can replace cathode with cheaper scrap.  We hear that scrap traders have been trying to maintain prices, rather than chase volume and therefore the discount is fluctuating in line with the rise and fall of LME prices.  So, should the price rally continue, we would expect to see scrap use continue to increase and displace some cathode consumption.  However, we expect this to be only at the margins.  One piece of supporting evidence for this view is that, despite the slowness of spot cathode business in the USA and Europe, premia have remained at the levels seen in July of 5.0-6.0¢/lb delivered East Coast in the US and $60-90/t cif Rotterdam in Europe. 

## **Disruptions continue to constrain mine output** 

Despite the well-publicised strikes by workers at mines in Chile recently, Q2 mine production reports show that the main factor disrupting mine output in Chile was further declines in ore grades.  It is clear that the recent labour issues are increasing cost pressure on miners, as they may set precedents for future collective labour negotiations.  In fact, some miners have invited workers to start negotiations on their contracts early. This would hopefully avoid unionised workers going on strike as part of the negotiation process, which is usually the case in Chile. 

The strike at Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, may have ended last month, but the threat of a strike at Grasberg, the world’s second largest mine, still hangs over the market this month.  The union at the mine has indicated that Freeport’s offer on the table is not acceptable and a strike is becoming more likely. Disruptions continue to dog mine output, with our latest estimate of the H1 disruption amounting to 890,000t compared to our January forecast of the planned production in the period.  In Q3 we expect to see mine disruptions amounting to almost 500,000t, or 100,000t more than we forecast at the start of the year. 

## **Prices to remain subject to financial and economic influences** 

LME open interest started rising when the copper price climbed in late July, signalling that market participants were opening long positions.  However, open interest fell during the early August sell-off, indicating these positions were subsequently liquidated – a signal that market sentiment had turned bearish. Unlike the other LME metals, copper did not see significant short selling as prices fell, though there may have been some build up in short positions.  The upturn in prices at the end of August has been accompanied by continued declines in open interest, which indicates short covering. 

It is too soon to disentangle the influences of the recent economic and financial market turmoil from any slowdown in consumption, given that it occurred in a seasonally slow period.  We do however believe that copper consumption will hold up, as the global economy muddles through the rest of the year before picking up again in 2012.  Having held above $8,50

2011, with consumption growing 6.5% y-o-y and 3.1% compared to H2 2010. Copper tube consumption in China was particularly robust, increasing by 11.5% y-o-y in H1, mainly supported by government subsidies for white appliances.  However, it was Japan that exceeded our growth expectations the most, achieving a rise in copper tube consumption of 20.4% y-o-y in H1, despite the negative impact of the 11<sup>th</sup> March earthquake and tsunami.  World Q2 consumption rose 1.9% y-o-y and 4.6% q-o-q, exhibiting steady growth. 

Japan’s 20.0% growth in copper tube consumption in Q2 proved to be the greatest surprise in this half of the year.  We had originally expected that the March disaster would have caused a significant reduction in both Q2 consumption and output, with recovery in the copper tube market not anticipated until H2 2011. It appears that reconstruction began earlier than originally anticipated, and as a consequence, Japan’s copper tube demand was boosted unexpectedly.  Moreover, Japan’s reconstruction activity also supported production in neighbouring copper tube producing countries such as South Korea, which experienced a 6.1% q-o-q jump in output in Q2. 

China’s strong performance in the copper tube sector was led primarily by government subsidies for the purchase of white goods, including air conditioners.  Sales of air conditioners grew by 60.7% y-o-y in H1 2011.  Around 25% of the manufacturing cost of each air conditioner is accounted for by copper components, in particular copper tube.  However, some of the aforementioned stimulus packages have been withdrawn in recent months and the air conditioner market seems to be approaching saturation point, leading us to believe that the growth in Chinese copper tube production and consumption is likely to slow in the second half of this year.  Moreover, the tighter Chinese credit market is likely to deter consumption activity further.  In addition, many air conditioner manufacturers, including GREE, Hisense and Haier, have recently increased their selling prices by RMB100-200 in response to rising costs, which they mainly attribute to high copper prices.  China’s copper tube production capacity nonetheless continues to increase further with the commissioning of projects like Chinalco’s 20,000t/y metal clad sheet manufacturing facility, which has dedicated one of its three production lines to the manufacture of copper and copper alloy tube. 

South and Central America experienced some of the highest growth rates in copper tube production and consumption worldwide in H1 2011.  Copper tube production rose by 16.5% y-o-y to 28,000t in H1, whereas consumption increased by 24.3% y-o-y to 32,000t.  Much of the increase in consumption is attributed to the Brazilian government’s copper-intensive housing and infrastructure development programmes currently in place.  Chile is one of the key suppliers of copper semis to the Brazilian market, favoured by the strong Brazilian real. 

Germany was amongst

the top performers in Western Europe, recording a 10.2% y-o-y rise in production to 80,000t and a 19.8% y-o-y increase in consumption to 40,000t in H1 2011. In contrast, Spain’s copper tube production and consumption declined by 15.4% and 7.6% respectively in H1 2011. We expect that as a result of the euro-zone debt crisis having the greatest impact on economies in Southern Europe, a dichotomy will continue to be apparent between the southern and northern copper sectors.  The copper tube sector in Eastern and Central Europe remained stable in H1, with production expanding 2.5% y-o-y and consumption growing by 0.1% y-o-y.

Copper tube production and consumption growth remains dominated by the US in North America.  The US anti-dumping duties on all imports of copper tube from China and Mexico continue to impact Mexican production, which contracted by 42.3% y-o-y in H1 2011.  In contrast, US copper tube output expanded by 14.1% y-o-y in H1 2011, however, it declined by 2.5% sequentially in Q2, mainly in response to debt worries and concerns of a double-dip recession. 

## **Copper alloy rod, bar and section sector remains stable** 

The world copper alloy rod, bar and section (RBS) sector remained stable in H1 2011, with production growing 2.3% y-o-y.  Q2 production fell by 1.3% y-o-y and q-o-q, attributed mainly to a slow-down in China’s economy and a tighter credit market.  However, North East Asia was the only major region to have experienced any significant change.  Copper alloy RBS production and consumption in the region experienced 22.3% y-o-y and 20.5% y-o-y growth respectively in H1 2011.  More interestingly, Japan witnessed a 1.9% q-o-q increase in production and a 6.8% q-o-q increase in consumption in Q2, despite the earthquake and tsunami in late Q2.  As discussed earlier, it appears that Japan’s reconstruction efforts are taking place at a faster pace than expected, thus generating significant demand for copper semis. Japan’s neighbour, South Korea, has also benefitted from the reconstruction activity, experiencing a 13.7% y-o-y increase in production in H1 2011. 

In addition, the production of brass bars in Japan is set for further increases with Kitz Metal Works’ announcement of plans to add a continuous casting line at their Chino plant.  The US$2.6M development will add a further 18,000-19,200t to the company’s annual billet production capacity. Construction work is set to begin this month and the plant is expected to be commissioned by the end of the year.  The expansion is also indicative of a recovering construction sector in Japan, in part supported by the disaster reconstruction efforts. 

In the US, Mueller Industries Inc., a leading copper alloy rod, bar and section and copper tube producer, expressed interest in expanding their production facilities as well as diversifying their product range. Mueller has p

laced a preliminary non-binding bid letter for the 100% purchase of unnamed copper producing assets based in Reading, Pennsylvania, owned by Industrias Unidas SA de CV and its subsidiary, United Copper Industries Inc. (UCI). Mueller has allocated US$35-50M in cash for the purchase. ## **Russian wirerod exports to the US rise sharply** Following Russia’s reintroduction of a 10% duty on cathode exports in February 2011, Russian wirerod exports increased sharply in Q2 2011, reflecting CRU’s earlier expectations. Wirerod exports totalled 91,816t in Q2 2011, up 105.9% y-o-y from 44,586t. Traditionally, Russia exports wirerod to the Netherlands, Germany and Turkey, however, we have observed that the US has become a key export destination for Russian material in recent months. In June 2011, the US imported 6,662t of wirerod from Russia, which accounts for 40.2% of total wirerod imports to the US that month. It would therefore appear that Russia is possibly shipping excess wirerod into the US market due to market saturation at its traditional export destinations. It is noteworthy that the US did not import any wirerod directly from Russia between April 2009 and April 2011, which is most likely the result of the changes to export duties in that time frame. We expect that this will impact US wirerod fabricators who will be faced with deflated domestic prices. - **Hellenic Cables S.A.** announced the acquisition of **Fulgor S.A.** through a 100% share purchase. Fulgor S.A. is a producer of cables, conductors and bare copper and aluminium wirerod, with significant experience in producing value added products such as high voltage and submarine cables.  Fulgor S.A.’s **Soussaki Corinth** plant has a production capacity of 50,000t/y of cables and conductors and 45,000t/y of copper and aluminium wirerod.  It was also announced that **PKC Group Oyj** , the Finnish wiring, cable and electronic manufacturer, signed an agreement to buy **AEES** , the North American wiring harness manufacturer, for €109M in cash and €1.25M in newlyissued PKC shares.  PKC principally produces wiring harnesses for the automotive industry in Europe and South America. 

- China’s **SWCC Showa Holdings Co. Ltd.** announced plans to construct a factory for copper wire rod production in China in the 2012 fiscal year. It plans to locate the new factory, which will have a production capacity of 60,000t/y, in Tianjin and to invest RMB1-1.5B. In China, high-quality copper wires are in demand because they are used in winding wires for automobiles and railroads. The company said it also plans to invest around RMB1.5 B in adding equipment to its factory in Zhejiang to double annual capacity there to 60,000t. 

- **Kitz Metal Works** , a brass bar maker and subsidiary of the **Kitz group** , announced plans to add a continuous casting line at its **Chino** plant in Japan.  The US$2.6M development will add a further 18,000t-19,200t to the company’s annual billet production capacity.  Construction work is set to begin this month and the plant is expected to be commissioned by the end of the year.  The company expects that the lower production cost of the new casting line will allow for the investment cost to be recovered within five years. 

- Switzerland-based power and automation technology group, **ABB Ltd.** , won a contract tendered by **TenneT** , the Dutch-German transmission grid operator, to connect North Sea wind farms to the German mainland grid.  The order is worth US$1.0B and ABB expect to use over 135km of 320kV submarine cable in the designed transmission system.  The project is expected to be operational in 2015 and follows two other offshore wind connection orders for ABB in Germany; the 800MW **Dolwin1** link awarded last year and previously, the **BorWin1** project which is due to service the **BARD Offshore 1** windfarm from 2012.  The Dolwin1 link is expected to be completed in 2013 and will involve the use of 150km of 320kV copper submarine cable. 

- **Nexans** reported that it saw strong improvement in performance in H1 2011.  The cable maker said that sales at current metal prices amounted to €2.3B in H1 2011, up by 8.9% y-o-y.  Despite this, the company announced a pre-tax loss of €133M compared with a €5M profit in

H1 2010.  This was mainly attributed to the inclusion of a €200M reserve relating to an ongoing E.U. proceeding for alleged anticompetitive behaviour in the submarine and underground power cable sector. The company realised an organic growth over the period of 8.2% y-o-y and said that all business units exhibited growth, especially the Industry and Building unit.  Nexans is targeting sales growth of between 5 and 7% for full year 2011. 

- The **National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS)** reported that the production growth rate of major domestic copper-using products, with the exception of electricity and air-conditioners, slowed y-o-y in H1 2011. The car industry was especially affected, with auto production growing by 5.1% in H1 2011, compared with 46.6% in H1 2010. Output of household refrigerators and household iceboxes was 9.5 and 23.1 percentage points lower y-o-y in H1 2011 respectively. In contrast, the growth rate of air-conditioners increased by 2.3 percentage points y-o-y to 41.8% in H1 2011. 

- **Changzhou Jinyuan Copper** , a Chinese subsidiary of **JX Nippon Mining & Metals** , announced plans to increase its wire drawing capacity from 18,000t/y to 30,000t/y by the end of 2012.  The firm draws 1.13-3.50mm diameter copper wire from 8.00mm wirerod and supplies it to Chinese winding

## **Mine Production** 











- Following failed wage negotiations at **Freeport-McMoRan** ’s **Grasberg** mine, the workers’ union has threatened the mine operator with strike action.  Workers were initially demanding that their wages  be increased to US$35-200/hr from the US$1.5-3/hr that they currently receive, however negotiations appear to be deadlocked at the moment.  Workers have already downed tools in protest of their low pay for nine consecutive days between 4<sup>th</sup> and 12<sup>th</sup> July.  Grasberg is expected to produce around 510,000t of copper-in-concentrate in 2011. 

- On 25<sup>th</sup> August, state-owned energy provider **Zesco** asked mining companies to temporarily reduce their electricity consumption due to a fault on a major power line.  The 400kV faulty power line is used to import electricity from South Africa via Zimbabwe.  In the interim, Zambian authorities have arranged to import 95MW of power from Mozambique to counter the shortfall.  The news was p

receded by a statement from Zambia’s **Copperbelt Energy Corporation (CEC)** on 24<sup>th</sup> August, in which they announced expectations of electricity costs nearly doubling by 2015 as a result of high capital costs associated with the development of the new generation plants.  The CEC is the main provider of power to mining companies in Zambia. 

- Workers at Chile’s **Escondida** mine agreed to end their two week strike over bonuses after reaching an agreement with **BHP Billiton** , the mine’s operator, on 5<sup>th</sup> August.  Workers accepted a bonus of US$5,760, which is significantly less than the US$11,000 bonus they initially demanded. The mine is believed to have suffered a 40,000t loss in contained copper production as a result of the strike and was forced to declare _force majeure_ on copper concentrate shipments.  Nevertheless, the hard line stance adopted by the company is of significant importance to any potential labour unrest this year, as it demonstrated that mining companies still retain sufficient power to quench workers’ demands _._ Escondida is expected to produce around 610,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 300,000t of EW cathode in 2011. 

- The **Collahuasi** mine workers’ union staged a 24-hour walkout on 30<sup>th</sup> July.  The union made demands for higher worker bonuses in keeping with the sentiments of the ongoing strikes at **Escondida** and an end to alleged anti-union measures by management.  However, reports state that many employees continued to work during the strike action and as such production was unaffected. Collahuasi is jointly owned by **Anglo American** and **Xstrata** with a Japanese consortium of investors holding a minority share.  Production in 2011 is expected to reach around 505,000t of copper-in-concentrate 35,000t of EW cathode **.** 

- **Kazakhmys Plc** announced that average copper ore grades at its operations in the Zhezkazgan region declined to 1.01% in H1 2011, falling from 1.14% a year earlier.  As a consequence, H1 production declined from 164,300t in H1 2010 to 153,000t in the same period this year. The company maintains that these operations are on target to reach the 300,000t production target for 2011.

## **Smelting and Refining** 



- China’s **Western Mining** has reported concentrate shortages which have caused the company to revise its expected output in 2011.  The company’s annual production guidance is down 21% for copper cathode from 58,000t.  In addition to this, **Guangdong Jiangmen** port returned two batches of copper concentrate deliveries that amounted to 696t, because they were found to consist of a large amount of soil.  Analysis of the deliveries from the Philippines showed them to consist of less than 1% copper and has since resulted in the port staff alerting other ports and authorities to help prevent unqualified shipments.
